title: No-Code Builder Lab: Apps & Automation
blurb: Two career-changing skills in one lab: turn a web project into a real Android APK using only your browser (from the Team21 MaDSkillz manual), and build your first business automation with Make or Zapier — no code, no command line, ever.

modules.d: The concepts behind the clicks — repositories, automated builds, web-to-Android packaging and safe distribution.
modules.body:
Why understand what happens behind the buttons

This lab will take you from a downloaded project to an Android app installed on a phone, and to a working business automation — without writing code or using a command line. Builders who understand what each step does fix problems faster, explain their work confidently, and grow into more advanced roles. This module gives you the mental model.

GitHub: your project's home in the cloud

GitHub is a platform used by millions of developers to store, version and collaborate on software projects. Key ideas: a repository (repo) is a project folder with its full history; a commit is a saved snapshot of changes with a message describing them; every commit can be viewed or reverted later, which is your safety net. A public repository can be seen by anyone — required in this lab for free automated builds and public download links — so never place passwords, private keys or personal data in it.

Automated builds: CI/CD

Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) means that every time you change your project, machines automatically build (and can test and package) it. GitHub's CI/CD service is GitHub Actions. The instructions live in a workflow file inside the hidden .github folder of your project. When you upload that folder, GitHub reads the instructions and builds your Android app on its own servers — downloading Node.js, the Java development kit and the Android SDK, building the web app, syncing it into an Android project and producing the installable file. That is why the .github folder is critical: without it, nothing builds.

From web app to Android app. Your project is a web application (HTML, JavaScript and a framework such as React). A tool called Capacitor wraps that web app inside a native Android shell, so it runs like an installed app with an icon on the phone. The same approach can later produce iOS apps. Many real-world apps use this "web inside native" model.

APK, AAB and distribution

An APK (Android Package) is the file Android installs directly — perfect for testing and sharing within your community. The Google Play Store requires new apps to be submitted as an Android App Bundle (AAB), along with a developer account, signing keys and store listing requirements; that is a later step. Installing an APK from outside the Play Store is called sideloading: Android asks permission ("Install from this source") because apps from unknown sources can be unsafe. Only install APKs you trust — such as one you built yourself. Note that Google has announced developer verification requirements for apps installed on certified Android devices, phasing in from 2026 in some countries; if you plan wider distribution outside the Play Store, check the current rules.

No-code automation

The second half of this lab uses Make or Zapier to connect apps. Every automation has three parts: a trigger (the event that starts it — a new form response), one or more actions (what happens — send an email), and data mapping (passing information from the trigger into the action — the respondent's name and email). This trigger–action–mapping pattern underlies thousands of business automations.

What you will have by the end

  • A GitHub account hosting your project with full version history.
  • An automated system that builds a fresh Android APK every time you change your app.
  • An installed app on your phone and a public download link others can use.
  • A working business automation and the design skills to build more.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my no-code mentor. Explain in simple language, with an everyday analogy for each, what a repository, a commit, a workflow file, GitHub Actions, Capacitor, an APK and an AAB are. Then quiz me with 5 short questions to check I understand how a change in my project becomes a new installable app.

📚 Glossary

  • Repository: project folder with full version history
  • Commit: saved snapshot of changes with a message
  • CI/CD: automatic building, testing and delivery on every change
  • GitHub Actions: GitHub's automation service that runs workflows
  • Capacitor: tool wrapping a web app inside a native mobile shell
  • APK / AAB: Android installable package / Play Store submission format
  • Sideloading: installing apps from outside the Play Store

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual: From Zero to Android APK in One Hour. Team21 Academy.
  • GitHub Docs — Repositories, commits and GitHub Actions.
  • Capacitor documentation (capacitorjs.com).
  • Android Developers — Android App Bundles; developer verification announcements (verify current status).

quiz.q: Amina, a trainer in Douala, edits her app's text directly on GitHub and the new version breaks the build. She wants yesterday's working wording back with the least risk. What should she do?
opts: Make a Release tagged v1.0.1 so users get a stable copy while she investigates
Edit the workflow file so the build skips the step that is now failing
Open file's History, view the last working commit and restore that content
Delete the repository and upload the original zip again as a fresh project
quiz.x: Every commit is a snapshot that can be viewed and restored, so History is the safety net. Re-uploading the zip also works but throws away all later good changes and the build history.

quiz.q: A youth NGO in Bamenda wants free automated APK builds and a public download link, but its project contains a config file with the SMS provider's private API key. What is the right setup?
opts: Make the repository private so the key stays hidden and builds still run for free
Keep the repository public and rename the key file so that it looks harmless
Upload publicly, then delete the key in a later commit once the build works
Keep the repository public and remove the key before uploading anything to it
quiz.x: The lab requires a public repo for free builds and public links, and secrets must not go into it. Deleting later is weaker: the key remains visible in commit history.

quiz.q: Kofi in Limbe uploads his project to GitHub. The files src, public and package.json appear, but nothing shows in the Actions tab after ten minutes. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The hidden .github folder with the workflow file was not part of the upload
His package.json lists a library that GitHub Actions cannot download today
The free GitHub build queue is busy and the run will start within the hour
Two-factor authentication is off, so GitHub refuses to start automated runs
quiz.x: Without .github/workflows there are no instructions, so no run ever appears. A failing dependency would still create a run that shows a red cross, not an empty Actions tab.

quiz.q: A Texas church volunteer asks why the course uses Capacitor when the project is already a working React web app. Which explanation best matches what Capacitor does in this pipeline?
opts: It hosts the React site online so phones can open it from a public web address
It wraps the built web app in a native Android shell installed with an icon
It signs the app with Google's keys so that it can be listed on the Play Store
It converts the React code into native Java so the app runs faster on phones
quiz.x: Capacitor packages the web build inside a native shell; the web code still runs inside it. Rewriting into native Java is a common misconception and not what the sync step does.

quiz.q: A startup in Yaoundé built an APK that testers love and now wants to publish on Google Play next month. Which statement about the file they will submit is correct?
opts: Play needs an iOS build too, because Capacitor apps must ship on both platforms
They submit the APK zipped exactly as it comes out of the GitHub Actions artifact
Play accepts the same APK if it is signed, since APK is Android's install format
New Play Store apps go in as an Android App Bundle with a developer account and signing
quiz.x: Since August 2021 Google Play requires new apps as AABs plus account, signing and listing. The signed-APK option is the runner-up because APKs still install fine by sideloading, just not for new Play listings.

quiz.q: A Lagos school tests an app by sending its APK over WhatsApp. Parents report Android blocking the install with a warning about the source. How should the school brief them?
opts: Tell them the file is damaged and resend it as a Google Drive link instead
Explain this is sideloading: allow installs from that source, then tap Install
Ask them to install from the Play Store, where the app is already published
Ask them to switch off Play Protect for the whole phone before installing
quiz.x: Installing outside the Play Store is sideloading, and Android asks permission per source. Switching off Play Protect globally removes a safety layer far beyond what is needed.

quiz.q: Grace sets up an automation: a Google Form submission sends a Gmail reply containing the respondent's first name. Which part is the data mapping?
opts: Inserting Name answer from the form into the email body
The schedule that controls how often Make checks the form
The Google Form receiving a new response from a customer
Gmail sending out the reply to the customer's inbox
quiz.x: Trigger, action and mapping make every automation; mapping is passing the respondent's data into the action. The schedule affects the trigger's timing, not the data passed along.

quiz.q: An instructor in Garoua changes one heading in App.jsx and commits. About ten minutes later she has a new APK without doing anything else. What made this happen?
opts: Capacitor watches the repository and rebuilds the app whenever a file is saved
The phone fetched the new version automatically from the repository overnight
A GitHub Actions workflow runs on each commit and rebuilds the app in the cloud
GitHub's editor exports an APK every time a file is edited in the browser window
quiz.x: CI/CD means each change triggers an automated build defined in the workflow file. Capacitor is one step inside that build; it does not watch the repo itself.

quiz.q: A Nairobi builder must explain to a manager what a commit is, in terms that justify writing clear messages like 'Update contact number'. Which description fits best?
opts: A saved snapshot of changes with a message, which can be viewed or reverted later
A backup of the whole repository stored offline on the developer's own computer
A build of the project produced by GitHub Actions and stored as an artifact file
A request asking GitHub to publish a new public release of the project for users
quiz.x: A commit is a snapshot plus a message, and that history is what makes reverting safe. A Release is a later, separate step that publishes a tagged version.

quiz.q: A US nonprofit asks why its volunteers should learn what each step does instead of just following screenshots. Which reason does the course give for building this mental model?
opts: Understanding the steps lets volunteers skip the Actions tab once builds work
GitHub requires a basic knowledge test before it lets accounts run Actions
Screenshots go out of date, and the mental model removes the need for any docs
Builders who understand each step fix problems faster and explain work clearly
quiz.x: The module argues understanding helps you troubleshoot and explain your work and grow into advanced roles. The 'no docs needed' option overstates it; documentation still matters.

facts.t: Developers on GitHub, as announced in early 2023.
facts.more: Your repository lives on the same platform professional teams use, which makes your build history a visible part of your portfolio.

facts.t: Every automation: trigger, action(s), data mapping.
facts.more: A new form response (trigger) sends an email (action) using the respondent's name and address (mapping). Thousands of business automations follow this pattern.

facts.t: Format Google Play requires for new apps since August 2021.
facts.more: APKs remain perfect for testing and sideloading; the Play Store needs an Android App Bundle plus a developer account and signing.

facts.t: The hidden folder that holds your build instructions.
facts.more: Without the workflow file inside .github/workflows, GitHub Actions has nothing to run — and no APK is ever built.

plaibox.title: Simulation: your first public project
plaibox.intro: You are setting up your first app project for a church youth group in Yaoundé. Make each call: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Well done: you protected secrets, kept your build pipeline intact and chose the right distribution format.
plaibox.lose: Review the mental model — public repos, the .github folder, APK vs AAB — and try again.

steps.s: Your app needs the group's admin password to send notifications. Where does it go?
o: Into App.jsx so the app works straight away
A public repository exposes it to anyone on the internet.
Nowhere in the repo; ask your mentor about a secure method
Never place passwords or keys in a public repository.
Into a separate file called secret.txt at the top of the repository
Better named, but still public and readable by anyone.

steps.s: To make the project look tidy, you consider deleting the faded .github folder.
o: Delete it — faded folders are system junk
Without .github, GitHub Actions has no instructions and nothing builds.
Keep it; it holds the build workflow
Right: the workflow file is what turns changes into APKs.
Move it into the src folder

steps.s: Youth members want the app this weekend. How do you distribute it?
o: Share the APK you built via a public release link
APKs are ideal for testing and community sharing you control.
Submit to the Play Store first
Valid later, but needs an AAB, developer account and review time.
Forward any APK a member finds online with a similar name
Unknown APKs can be unsafe; only share what you built.

modules.t: Zero to Android APK I: GitHub & Your Project
modules.d: Create your account, prepare your files with hidden folders visible, and create the repository correctly.
modules.body:
What you are about to do

Take a downloaded project file and turn it into a real Android app you can install on any phone — without touching a command line. First time through: about 45 minutes. Every time after: about 10 minutes.

Step 1 — Set up GitHub (5 min)

Open github.com in any modern browser and click Sign up. Use a real email address you check, a strong unique password, and a professional username — it becomes part of your public URLs (github.com/yourname) and potentially your professional portfolio. Verify the email code (check spam for messages from GitHub) and skip optional personalisation questions. Turn on two-factor authentication in your security settings — strongly recommended, and increasingly required by GitHub for contributors.

Step 2 — Prepare your files (3 min)

The project arrives as a compressed zip. Extract it: on Windows, right-click the zip in Downloads → Extract All → Extract; on Mac, double-click the zip. Open the extracted folder.

Critical: show hidden files. The project contains a .github folder. Names starting with a dot are hidden by default. Windows: in File Explorer, View → Show → Hidden items. Mac: press Command + Shift + . (period). The .github folder will appear slightly faded.

Critical checkpoint. Confirm you can SEE the .github folder before continuing. If you cannot see it, you cannot upload it — and your APK will never build. This single step causes more first-time failures than any other.

Understand what is in the folder

  • src — the app's source code, including App.jsx, which holds the app's text and interface.
  • public — static files such as icons and images.
  • package.json — the list of tools and libraries the project uses (do not edit unless you know why).
  • .github/workflows — the build instructions for GitHub Actions.
  • Capacitor configuration — settings for packaging the web app as an Android app (app name, ID).

Step 3 — Create the repository (5 min)

Signed in to GitHub, click the + icon (top right) → New repository. Name it in lowercase with dashes (for example madskillz-ai-readiness) — no spaces. Add a short description. Choose Public (required for free builds and public download links in this lab). Leave "Add a README", ".gitignore" and "license" unchecked — your project already contains its files, and adding them here creates conflicts. Click Create repository.

Naming and professionalism

Your repository and username are visible to anyone, including future employers and clients. Clear names, a description and later a README explaining what the app does make your work look professional and trustworthy.

Common mistakes at this stage

  • Uploading the zip file itself instead of the extracted contents.
  • Uploading the outer folder, so all files end up one level too deep.
  • Not showing hidden files, so .github is missed.
  • Ticking README or license options and creating conflicts.
  • Choosing Private, which blocks the lab's free public release links.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my GitHub setup guide. Walk me through creating my account, enabling two-factor authentication, showing hidden files on my operating system (I will tell you which), and creating my repository — one step at a time, waiting for me to confirm each step. At the end, give me a checklist to confirm the .github folder is visible and the repository settings are correct.

📚 Glossary

  • Two-factor authentication: second verification step protecting your account
  • Hidden files: files or folders starting with a dot, not shown by default
  • App.jsx: main app file holding text and interface
  • package.json: list of project tools and libraries
  • README: document explaining a project

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual, Parts 1–3. Team21 Academy.
  • GitHub Docs — Creating a new repository; Configuring two-factor authentication.

quiz.q: Thierry in Bafoussam is creating his GitHub account for the lab and plans to share his app with clients. Which username choice best follows the module's advice?
opts: His company's full legal name with spaces, matching the business registration
A playful nickname, since he can rename the account once the app is popular
A professional name such as thierry-ngu, since it appears in public URLs
A random string of letters, so that clients cannot trace the account to him
quiz.x: The username becomes part of github.com/yourname URLs and the portfolio. Renaming later is possible but breaks shared links, so the playful option is the tempting runner-up.

quiz.q: After unzipping the project on Windows, Fatima sees src, public and package.json but no .github folder. What should she do before going any further?
opts: Download the zip again, since a missing .github means it was damaged
Turn on View, Show, Hidden items in File Explorer and confirm .github appears
Continue uploading and add the workflow file later through GitHub's editor
Rename package.json to .github so that GitHub can find the build steps
quiz.x: Dot-folders are hidden by default; showing hidden items is the critical checkpoint. Adding the workflow later can work but is error-prone and is not what the lab prescribes.

quiz.q: A Mac user in Abidjan cannot see the .github folder in Finder after extracting the project. Which action reveals it so it can be selected for upload?
opts: Open the folder in Safari, which lists hidden folders by default
Press Command + A in Finder, which selects and shows hidden files
Press Command + Shift + period in Finder to toggle hidden files on
Right-click the folder and choose Get Info to show its hidden items
quiz.x: Command + Shift + . toggles hidden files in Finder. Command + A is the runner-up because it is used later to select everything, but it does not reveal hidden items.

quiz.q: Joseph creates his repository and ticks 'Add a README' and '.gitignore' to look professional. Why does the lab tell him to leave those boxes unchecked?
opts: Repositories that contain a README cannot run free builds on GitHub Actions
His project already has its files, and adding these here creates conflicts
A .gitignore stops the hidden .github folder from being uploaded later
Ticking them makes the repository private, which blocks public downloads
quiz.x: The project arrives complete, and GitHub-generated starter files create conflicts with the upload. The .gitignore option sounds technical but is not the reason given.

quiz.q: A Chicago team names a new repo for its reading app. Which name follows the lab's naming convention for repositories?
opts: Reading App Final Version 2
ReadingApp_FINAL_v2_copy
readingapp.final
chicago-reading-app
quiz.x: Lowercase words joined by dashes, with no spaces, give clean public URLs. readingapp.final is lowercase but uses a dot and an unclear name, so it is the weaker choice.

quiz.q: A training manager in Kumba wants to change the welcome text in the app. Inside the project folder, which file should she look in first?
opts: src/App.jsx, which holds the app's text and interface
package.json, which lists the tools and libraries the project uses
The Capacitor configuration, which stores the app name and app ID
The workflow file in .github, which describes the build stages
quiz.x: App.jsx in src holds the interface and text. The Capacitor configuration is the runner-up: it controls the app name on the phone, not on-screen welcome text.

quiz.q: Ngozi, a consultant in Accra, sets up GitHub for client work. She has a strong unique password. What extra security step does the module strongly recommend, and why?
opts: Make the repository private, since public code makes the account easier to hijack
Use her personal email instead of work email, so that alerts reach her faster
Turn on two-factor authentication, since a hijacked account could publish harmful APKs
Change her password monthly, since GitHub expires passwords after ninety days
quiz.x: 2FA is strongly recommended and increasingly required for contributors. Making the repo private conflicts with the lab's free-build setup and does not protect the account login.

quiz.q: A first-time learner in Buea asks how long the full process will take on her first try versus later updates. Which estimate matches the course?
opts: About 45 minutes each time, since every build downloads the toolkit again
About 45 minutes the first time and about 10 minutes for each later update
About 2 hours the first time, because the Android SDK must be installed
About 10 minutes the first time and about 45 minutes for each later update
quiz.x: Setup is about 45 minutes once; later updates take about 10 because the cloud pipeline does the heavy lifting. The 2-hour option assumes local SDK installation, which this lab avoids.

quiz.q: A recruiter in Washington DC browses a candidate's GitHub before an interview. Why does the module say naming and professionalism matter for repositories?
opts: Unprofessional names are flagged by GitHub and their builds are slowed
Recruiters may run automated checks on repo names before reading any code
GitHub ranks public repositories by name quality in its search results for recruiters
Repo and user names are public and can become part of a visible portfolio
quiz.x: Names appear in public URLs and are visible to anyone, so they form part of your professional profile. The automated-check option is speculative and not taught.

quiz.q: Paul extracts the project zip on Windows by double-clicking it and starts dragging files from the zip window to GitHub. What is the better approach according to Step 2?
opts: Right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then work in the extracted folder
Drag from the zip window but first switch on hidden items in its view
Rename the zip to .github so GitHub reads it as the build instructions
Upload the zip as one file, since GitHub extracts archives on its own
quiz.x: Step 2 says to extract properly and open the extracted folder. Showing hidden items is needed too, but working inside the compressed view is unreliable, so that option is incomplete.

facts.t: First full run from zip to installed app.
facts.more: About 10 minutes for every later update — the cloud pipeline does the heavy lifting after setup.

facts.t: Mac shortcut to show hidden files in Finder.
facts.more: On Windows: File Explorer → View → Show → Hidden items. Seeing .github before upload prevents the most common first-time failure.

facts.t: Two-factor authentication: a second check beyond your password.
facts.more: GitHub has rolled out mandatory 2FA for code contributors since 2023. Turn it on now; a hijacked account can publish harmful APKs under your name.

facts.t: Repository names: lowercase with dashes, no spaces.
facts.more: e.g. madskillz-ai-readiness. The name appears in public URLs, so it doubles as part of your professional profile.

modules.t: Zero to Android APK II: Upload, Build & Install
modules.d: Upload correctly, watch GitHub Actions build your app, and install it on a phone.
modules.body:
Step 4 — Upload your project (10 min)

On your empty repository page, click the link "uploading an existing file". Arrange your project folder window and your browser side by side. Inside the project folder, select everything (Ctrl + A on Windows, Command + A on Mac) and confirm the .github folder is highlighted. Drag the selection into GitHub's upload area. If GitHub warns that a file is hidden, continue — it is supposed to be.

Scroll down to Commit changes, type a short message such as "Initial upload of project", and click Commit changes. Then verify on the repository page that src, public, .github and package.json appear at the top level.

Step 5 — Watch the build (Actions tab)

The moment .github lands, GitHub starts building your app. Click the Actions tab, then the run named "Build Android APK" (it may show a spinning yellow icon). Watch each step turn green:

  1. Checkout — GitHub copies your code to a build machine.
  2. Set up Node.js — the JavaScript runtime used to build the web app.
  3. Set up Java JDK — needed for Android builds.
  4. Set up Android SDK — Android's development toolkit.
  5. Install dependencies — the libraries listed in package.json.
  6. Build web app — compiles the app into optimised files (the dist folder).
  7. Capacitor sync — copies the web build into the Android project.
  8. Build APK — produces the Android package.
  9. Upload artifact — stores the APK for you to download.

The first build usually takes 5–10 minutes because GitHub downloads the full Android toolkit; later builds are faster. You can close the page — the build continues.

Read the log like a detective. If a step shows a red ❌, click it. The log shows exactly which command failed and the error message. The error message is your best clue — the troubleshooting module maps common messages to fixes. A red ❌ is normal in software work and almost always fixable.

Step 6 — Download and install (5 min)

On the successful run's page, scroll to Artifacts and click the artifact name to download a zip. Unzip it to find the .apk file. Transfer it to your Android phone by email, Google Drive, messaging app or USB cable.

On the phone, open the file from your Files or Downloads app. Android will warn that installing from this source is not allowed — tap Settings, enable Allow from this source, go back and tap Install, then Open. The app requires Android 8.0 or newer.

What you just achieved

You have built and installed a real Android app using a professional cloud build pipeline — the same kind of CI/CD system used by software teams worldwide — without installing developer tools. That is a genuine builder credential.

Security habits

After installing, consider turning "Allow from this source" off again for apps like your file manager or browser, so other unknown apps cannot install silently. Only share APKs that you built or trust, and tell testers where the file came from.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my build-log interpreter. I will paste the steps and any error text from my GitHub Actions run. Explain in simple language what each step does, identify the failed step and the likely cause, and give me the exact browser-only fix to try first, then a second option if that fails.

📚 Glossary

  • Workflow run: one execution of the build instructions
  • Artifact: file produced and stored by a workflow run
  • dist folder: compiled, optimised web app output
  • Capacitor sync: copying the web build into the native project
  • Build log: detailed record of each build step and errors

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual, Parts 4–6. Team21 Academy.
  • GitHub Docs — Viewing workflow run history; Downloading workflow artifacts.
  • Android Help — Install apps from unknown sources (varies by manufacturer).

quiz.q: Mireille uploads her project, and the repository page shows src, public and package.json at the top level, but .github sits inside a folder named madskillz-main. What happened, and what is the fix?
opts: GitHub moves hidden folders into subfolders; move .github to the top later
The workflow is fine wherever it sits; wait for the Actions tab to start
She forgot a commit message; add one now so GitHub reorganises the folders
She dragged parent folder instead of its contents; re-upload the contents
quiz.x: Workflows must sit at .github/workflows in the repo root, so the contents need uploading, not the parent folder. Moving it later works in principle but GitHub does not relocate it on its own.

quiz.q: While dragging files into GitHub's upload area, Eric gets a warning that one item is a hidden file. According to Step 4, what should he do?
opts: Continue, because hidden .github folder is supposed to be uploaded
Cancel the upload and rename .github so that it is no longer hidden
Switch to the GitHub mobile app, which does not show this warning
Remove the hidden item from the selection and upload the rest first
quiz.x: The warning is expected; .github is meant to be hidden and must be uploaded. Renaming it would break the build because GitHub looks for exactly .github.

quiz.q: In the Actions log, the step 'Set up Java JDK' is green but 'Build web app' shows a red cross. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
opts: Capacitor sync failed, so the APK cannot be created from this project
The web build failed, likely because of an error in app's source code
GitHub's build machine was offline, so the whole run should be retried
The Android SDK was missing, so later Android steps did not start
quiz.x: The failing step names the problem: the web build, usually a code typo. Retrying is the runner-up instinct, but the log shows an earlier step succeeded, so the machine was working.

quiz.q: A Houston volunteer's first build has been running for seven minutes with a yellow spinner, and he wants to go to lunch. What does the course say?
opts: Disconnect from Wi-Fi to pause the run and resume it after lunch
Cancel and restart it, since a first build longer than five minutes is stuck
Go to lunch; first builds take 5 to 10 minutes and continue if page closes
Keep the page open, because closing it cancels the run on GitHub's servers
quiz.x: First builds commonly take 5 to 10 minutes while GitHub downloads the toolkit, and runs continue in the cloud. Restarting a normal run just wastes time.

quiz.q: A learner asks why the build log has a step called 'Capacitor sync' after 'Build web app'. Which description of that step is correct?
opts: It installs the libraries listed in package.json on the build machine
It checks out the latest commit so the build uses the newest source code
It copies the compiled web build into the Android project for packaging
It uploads the finished APK so that it appears under Artifacts on GitHub
quiz.x: Capacitor sync copies the dist web build into the Android project. 'Install dependencies' handles package.json, and 'Upload artifact' stores the APK.

quiz.q: After a successful build, Halima downloads the artifact and sees a .zip file, not an .apk. Her colleague says the build went wrong. What is accurate?
opts: Artifacts download zipped, so she unzips it to find the .apk inside
The colleague is right; an APK artifact should arrive as a bare .apk file
The zip is an AAB, so she must convert it on a computer before use
She should rename the .zip to .apk so that Android can install it
quiz.x: Artifacts download as zips; unzipping reveals the .apk. Renaming the zip is tempting since an APK is itself zip-format, but the artifact zip contains the APK rather than being one.

quiz.q: A grandmother in Ebolowa installs the APK, but the app closes instantly every time she opens it. The same APK works on her grandson's newer phone. What should be checked first?
opts: Whether the APK was downloaded from Artifacts instead of a Release link
Whether she allowed installation from the source before tapping Install
Whether her Google account has two-factor authentication switched on
Whether its Android version, in Settings, is 8.0 or above
quiz.x: The app needs Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer, and crashes on open point there. The install-permission option is the runner-up, but the app did install, so that step already passed.

quiz.q: A trainer distributes an APK at a workshop. Which order of phone steps matches the course when Android warns that the source is not allowed?
opts: Tap Install, then Open, then go to Settings to allow the source
Tap Settings, enable Allow from this source, go back, tap Install
Tap Settings, then Install, then enable Allow from this source
Enable Play Protect, then tap Install, then allow from this source
quiz.x: The prompt leads to Settings to allow the source, then back to Install and Open. Installing before permission is granted fails, so the first option has the steps out of order.

quiz.q: The build log for a run lists nine stages. A learner says the build is 'just compiling the app'. Which stage list shows why that is incomplete?
opts: Checkout, dependencies, APK, sync, web build, JDK, SDK, Node.js, artifact
Checkout, web build, Play signing, store listing, APK, release, artifact
Node.js, Capacitor install, iOS build, APK, AAB, store upload, artifact
Checkout, Node.js, JDK, SDK, dependencies, web build, sync, APK, artifact
quiz.x: The nine steps run from checkout through toolkit setup, web build, sync, APK and upload. The last option has the right names in the wrong order; sync must follow the web build.

quiz.q: A Cameroon school IT lead uploads, commits with the message 'stuff', and the build succeeds. What would the course suggest improving next time?
opts: Nothing, since commit messages matter mainly when the build fails
Write a short descriptive message such as 'Initial upload of project'
Put the version number in the message so that a Release is created
Leave the message empty so that GitHub fills in the default text
quiz.x: Clear messages make history readable, which matters when you later need to revert. Version numbers belong in Release tags, not in commit messages, so that option misplaces them.

facts.t: Typical duration of the first build.
facts.more: GitHub downloads Node.js, the Java JDK and the Android SDK the first time. You can close the page — the build continues in the cloud.

facts.t: Minimum Android version this app requires.
facts.more: Android 8.0 (Oreo) is API level 26. If the app crashes on open, check Settings → About phone first.

facts.t: Stages in the 'Build Android APK' run.
facts.more: Checkout, Node.js, Java JDK, Android SDK, dependencies, web build, Capacitor sync, APK build, artifact upload. A red ❌ tells you exactly which one failed.

facts.t: An APK is a zip-format package; artifacts download zipped too.
facts.more: That is why you unzip the downloaded artifact to find the .apk file before transferring it to the phone.

labs.title: Follow the build pipeline
labs.intro: Put the GitHub Actions steps in the order they run.
steps: Checkout — copy code to a build machine
Set up Node.js
Set up Java JDK and Android SDK
Install dependencies from package.json
Build web app into the dist folder
Capacitor sync into the Android project
Build APK
Upload artifact
labs.tip: Web first, then wrap in Android. A failure in 'Build web app' causes a later 'no dist' error.

labs.title: Where should you look?
labs.intro: Match each situation to the first thing you should check.
pairs: Actions tab shows no run after upload
Whether .github reached the top level of the repo
All files are inside one extra folder
You uploaded the outer folder instead of its contents
Repository shows only a single .zip file
You uploaded the zip instead of extracting it
A step shows a red ❌
The log of that step for the error message
Phone refuses to install the file
The 'Allow from this source' setting for that app
labs.tip: Read the evidence first — the log or the file list — before changing anything.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the build that went red
plaibox.intro: You uploaded your project for a Bamenda youth NGO and the build failed. Make each call: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Calm, methodical debugging — exactly how professional teams handle a red build.
plaibox.lose: Revisit reading logs, checking the file layout and safe installs, then retry.

steps.s: The run shows a red ❌. What do you do first?
o: Delete the repository and start over
Drastic and loses the evidence; most failures are small fixes.
Click the failed step and read its error
The error message is your best clue.
Re-upload every project file again and hope it works this time
Might work by luck, but you learn nothing about the cause.

steps.s: The log says 'No such file or directory: dist'. What does it mean?
o: The web build failed earlier — scroll up
The dist folder is missing because 'Build web app' failed first.
GitHub's build servers are probably down right now
An outage looks different; this points to your project.
The APK step needs a new Android SDK
The APK step is a symptom here, not the cause.

steps.s: The build is green. A tester asks you to send the APK by WhatsApp. How do you prepare it?
o: Send the downloaded artifact zip and let them sort it out themselves
Works for some, but confuses testers who can't unzip on a phone.
Ask them to download from the Actions tab
Artifacts require a GitHub login — most testers won't have one.
Unzip the artifact and send the .apk with a note on its source
Clear, safe sharing: they know what it is and where it came from.

steps.s: After installing, what about 'Allow from this source' on your file manager?
o: Turn it off again
Stops other unknown apps from installing silently.
Leave it on for future builds
Convenient, but it leaves a door open for unsafe apps.
Also enable it for the browser
Widens the risk without any benefit.

modules.t: Zero to Android APK III: Releases, Updates & Troubleshooting
modules.d: Public download links, safe updates, version discipline and calm troubleshooting.
modules.body:
Step 7 — Create a public download link (Releases)

Artifacts require a GitHub login to download, so they are not ideal for sharing. A Release creates a permanent public download page anyone can open without an account. On your repository page: Releases → Create a new release → create a tag v1.0.0 → add a title and description ("First public release. Requires Android 8.0+") → Publish release. In this project, publishing the tag triggers a fresh build; about five minutes later the APK appears under Assets. Share the link (github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/your-repo/releases) on WhatsApp or social media, or print it as a QR code.

Step 8 — Making changes forever after

Navigate to any file in your repository (for example src/App.jsx), click the pencil icon, edit it in the browser like a document — your contact information, programme names, colours or text — then Commit changes with a clear message ("Update contact number"). A new APK builds automatically. Make one small change at a time and check the build succeeds before the next change; this makes errors easy to find.

Version discipline: semantic versioning

Versions communicate what changed: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. v1.0.0 → v1.0.1 for small fixes; → v1.1.0 for new features that do not break existing use; → v2.0.0 for major redesigns or breaking changes. Write release notes describing what changed so users and testers know what to expect.

Your safety net: history. Every commit is recorded. If an edit breaks the build, open the file's History, view the previous working version, and restore its content. Never panic about a broken build — the last working version is always there.

Step 9 — Troubleshooting the calm way

  • Red ❌ with "Could not find installation of TypeScript": replace capacitor.config.ts with capacitor.config.json containing the equivalent settings (your instructor provides the contents).
  • "Dependencies lock file is not found": edit the workflow file — remove the cache: npm line and change npm ci to npm install.
  • "No such file or directory: dist": the web build failed earlier — scroll up in the log; usually a typo in your last edit. Revert using file history.
  • Empty Artifacts: the build is still running or failed — check for a ❌.
  • "Allow from this source" missing: the setting location varies by brand; on stock Android try Settings → Apps → Special app access → Install unknown apps.
  • App crashes on open: the phone is probably below Android 8.0 — check Settings → About phone.
  • Uploaded the wrong files: you can delete the repository (Settings → Delete this repository) and start fresh.

The improvement loop

When you finish: test every feature; share the release link with at least three people; watch them install and use the app; note where they get confused; make one improvement; release v1.0.1; repeat. This build–measure–learn loop is how every great app evolves.

Next steps as a builder

Add a README describing your app, its purpose and how to install it. Later steps include custom app icons and names, publishing to the Play Store (requiring an AAB, a developer account and signing), and learning enough code to customise features with AI assistance in Vibe Coding Mastery.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my release manager. I will describe the changes I made to my app since the last release. Recommend the correct semantic version number (patch, minor or major) with reasoning, write clear release notes for testers in English and French, and give me a 5-step test checklist to run on my phone before sharing the release link.

📚 Glossary

  • Release: public, versioned download page
  • Tag: label marking a specific version, e.g., v1.0.0
  • Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbering
  • Release notes: description of what changed in a version
  • File history: record of every version of a file

📖 References

  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual, Parts 7–9. Team21 Academy.
  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — semver.org.
  • GitHub Docs — Managing releases in a repository.

quiz.q: A Douala health NGO wants to share its APK with 200 community workers who do not have GitHub accounts. Which approach does the module recommend?
opts: Publish a Release with tag v1.0.0 and share the public releases link
Email the unzipped APK to each worker from the instructor's own inbox
Send everyone the Actions artifact link from the latest successful build
Make each worker a GitHub account so they can download the artifacts
quiz.x: Releases give a permanent public page without login, while artifacts require an account. Emailing works for a few people but does not scale or give a stable link.

quiz.q: A US library app is at v1.4.2. The team adds an offline reading mode that does not change any existing features. What should the next version be?
quiz.x: A compatible new feature bumps MINOR and resets PATCH: v1.5.0. v1.4.3 is the runner-up but patch numbers are for fixes, not new features.

quiz.q: Version v2.3.7 of a Kenyan farm app is in use. The team fixes a typo in the price screen and nothing else. Which version should the fix ship as?
quiz.x: A small fix increments PATCH only: v2.3.8. v2.4.0 would signal a new feature, which overstates the change for testers.

quiz.q: A builder's latest commit breaks the build with 'No such file or directory: dist'. What does the troubleshooting guide say this usually means?
opts: The Capacitor config is in TypeScript and must be switched to JSON
The dist folder was not uploaded, so upload it manually from the zip
The web build failed earlier, usually from a typo in the last edit
The Android SDK download failed, so restart the run later in the day
quiz.x: Missing dist means the web build failed earlier; scroll up and revert the typo. Uploading dist manually treats the symptom and the next build would fail again.

quiz.q: A Kampala builder's first run fails with 'Dependencies lock file is not found'. What fix does Step 9 prescribe?
opts: Remove cache: npm line and change npm ci to npm install in the workflow
Upload a package-lock.json copied from any other React project online
Replace capacitor.config.ts with capacitor.config.json from the instructor
Delete package.json so that the workflow stops looking for a lock file
quiz.x: Without a lock file, npm ci and caching fail, so the workflow must use npm install. The Capacitor JSON swap fixes a different error about TypeScript.

quiz.q: Sandrine wants to change her phone number, the programme name and the colour scheme in App.jsx this afternoon. Which way of working does the module advise?
opts: Make all three changes in one commit so just one build runs today
Make one change per commit and check the build passes before the next
Edit the workflow file first so builds skip checks for small text edits
Make the changes on a computer and upload the whole project again
quiz.x: One change at a time shows exactly which edit broke a build. Batching saves builds but makes the cause of a failure hard to find, which is why it is the runner-up.

quiz.q: Publishing tag v1.0.0 in this project triggers a fresh build. A learner refreshes the Release page right away and sees no APK under Assets. What is the best interpretation?
opts: The build is likely still running; the APK appears after about five minutes
The tag was wrong; Releases must be named release-1 for builds to start
Releases do not hold APKs, so she should share the artifact link instead
She must attach the APK by hand, since Releases do not trigger builds here
quiz.x: In this project publishing the tag triggers a build, and the APK appears after about five minutes. Manual attachment is possible on GitHub generally but is not how this project works.

quiz.q: A testing team in Atlanta receives v1.1.0 with no description. Two testers waste a day re-testing unchanged screens. What practice would have helped most?
opts: Sending the APK through artifacts so testers see the build log
Holding the release until all features for v2.0.0 are complete
Releasing as v2.0.0 so testers know to re-test every screen
Writing release notes that describe what changed in the version
quiz.x: Release notes tell testers what to expect and where to focus. Bumping to v2.0.0 would misstate the change under semantic versioning.

quiz.q: A user with a Tecno phone cannot find 'Allow from this source' when installing. Which guidance from the troubleshooting list fits best?
opts: The APK is damaged and the user should download it again from Assets
The location varies by brand; on stock Android try Special app access
The user must first enable developer options before any sideloading works
The phone is below Android 8.0, so the app will not run at all on it
quiz.x: The setting's location differs between brands; Settings, Apps, Special app access, Install unknown apps is the stock path. Developer options are not required for sideloading.

quiz.q: Build fails with 'Could not find installation of TypeScript'. Which fix matches the troubleshooting guide?
opts: Change npm ci to npm install and remove the cache line in the workflow
Add TypeScript to package.json and rerun the workflow after commit
Replace capacitor.config.ts with an equivalent capacitor.config.json
Revert App.jsx to its previous version using the file History view
quiz.x: The guide swaps the TypeScript config for a JSON one supplied by the instructor. Adding TypeScript could work for an expert but changes dependencies the lab says not to edit.

facts.t: Semantic versioning format.
facts.more: Patch for fixes, minor for compatible features, major for breaking changes. Release notes tell testers what to expect.

facts.t: The tag that publishes your first release.
facts.more: In this project, publishing the tag triggers a fresh build; about five minutes later the APK appears under Assets on a public page.

facts.t: Releases download without a GitHub account; artifacts don't.
facts.more: Share the releases link on WhatsApp or as a printed QR code — anyone can install.

facts.t: Make one small change per commit, then check the build.
facts.more: If something breaks, you know exactly which edit caused it, and file History restores the last working version.

labs.title: Patch, minor or major?
labs.intro: Your app is at v1.2.0. Classify each change by the version it should produce.
items: Fix a typo in the French welcome text
Correct the wrong WhatsApp contact number
Fix a button that did nothing on small screens
Add a new quiz section while keeping the old ones
Add an option to share results with a mentor
Redesign the app so old saved results no longer load
Replace the whole navigation and data format
labs.tip: Ask: does it break what users already rely on? If yes, it's major.

labs.title: Error message to fix
labs.intro: Match each build or install problem to its documented fix.
pairs: Could not find installation of TypeScript
Replace capacitor.config.ts with the JSON version
Dependencies lock file is not found
Remove the npm cache line and switch to npm install
No such file or directory: dist
Find the earlier web-build error, often a typo — revert via History
Artifacts section is empty
Wait for the run to finish or look for a failed step
App crashes immediately on open
Check the phone runs Android 8.0 or newer
Uploaded the wrong files entirely
Delete the repository in Settings and start fresh
labs.tip: Calm troubleshooting: read the message, apply the mapped fix, change one thing at a time.

plaibox.title: Release notes builder
plaibox.intro: Prepare your next release. Fill the fields and copy the result into GitHub's release description.

fields.label: What changed (one per line)
fields.ph:
e.g. fixed contact number
improved French text

fields.label: Who tested it and how
fields.ph: e.g. 3 youth leaders installed it on Tecno and Samsung phones

fields.label: Known issues
fields.ph: e.g. dark mode not yet supported

checks.label: Testing names how many people or devices

plaibox.tip: Clear notes build trust. Publish, then share the release link with at least three testers.

modules.t: Your First Business Automation: Form → Instant Email
modules.d: Build a real automation with Make or Zapier, mapping form data into a personalised email.
modules.body:
What we are building

Someone fills out your Google Form → the automation sees the submission → they instantly receive a personalised thank-you email. No manual work. Real example: a yoga instructor's class registration automatically sends class details, location and time to each person who signs up.

Before you start

You need a Google account, Gmail to send replies, a Google Form, and a free account on Make (make.com) or Zapier (zapier.com).

Step 1 — Create the form

Go to Google Forms → create a blank form (e.g., "Customer Inquiry Form"). Add at least two short-answer questions: "What is your name?" and "What is your email?". The email field is essential — it is how the automation knows whom to reply to. Consider using response validation to require a valid email format. Preview the form to test it.

Option A — Make

  1. Log in to Make → Create a new scenario.
  2. Add the trigger module: search Google Forms → Watch Responses → create a connection to your Google account and allow access → select your form.
  3. Click + to add an action: Gmail → Send an Email → connect Gmail.
  4. To: click in the field and select the form's email answer from the mapping panel (the data the trigger provides).
  5. Subject: "Thank you for your inquiry!"; Content: your message — insert the respondent's name by selecting the Name field from the mapping panel.
  6. Save → Run once → submit the form yourself → check the email arrives.
  7. Turn the scenario ON and set its schedule (how often Make checks for new responses).

Option B — Zapier

  1. Log in to Zapier → Create → Zap.
  2. Trigger: Google Forms → New Form Response → connect your account → choose the form → submit a test response → Test trigger.
  3. Action: Gmail → Send Email → connect Gmail.
  4. Map To to the email answer; write the subject; in the body insert the Name field from the form data.
  5. Test action → check your inbox → name the Zap ("Form auto-reply") → Publish.
The most common mistake. Typing an email address or name into the field instead of selecting the mapped data. If you type text, every email goes to the same address with the same name. Always use the field selector to map form data.

Make or Zapier?

Both connect thousands of apps and offer free plans with usage limits. Zapier is often considered the simplest for beginners; Make offers a visual scenario builder that many find powerful for multi-step workflows and a generous free tier. Both count usage (Zapier in tasks; Make in operations or credits), and plans and limits change — check current pricing before building many automations.

Troubleshooting

  • No email sent: check that the Gmail connection shows as connected, the form has an email field, the scenario or Zap is ON, and check spam.
  • Name or email missing: you typed text instead of mapping the form field.
  • Google connection error: disconnect and reconnect, and confirm you are using the Google account that owns the form.

Responsible automation

Tell people in the form what will happen with their data and that they will receive an email. Collect only what you need, and protect respondents' information. Automated emails must still be accurate and respectful — test them as carefully as messages you write by hand.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my automation tutor. I want to build a Google Form → Gmail auto-reply in [Make or Zapier]. Walk me through each step one at a time, waiting for me to confirm. Then help me write a warm, bilingual (English and French) auto-reply email that includes the respondent's name and the next steps, and give me a 4-point test checklist before I switch it on.

📚 Glossary

  • Scenario / Zap: an automation in Make / Zapier
  • Module: a single step in a Make scenario
  • Mapping panel: where you select data from earlier steps
  • Task / operation: usage units counted by Zapier / Make
  • Response validation: form rule requiring correctly formatted answers

📖 References

  • Team21 Academy, No-Code Automation Guide: Automate Google Form Submissions with Instant Email Replies.
  • Make Help Center and Make Academy (make.com).
  • Zapier Help Center (zapier.com/help).
  • Google Forms Help — response validation.

quiz.q: A Yaoundé hair salon builds a Make scenario: Google Form to Gmail. Every customer gets an email addressed to 'Dear Brenda' sent to the owner's address. What went wrong?
opts: The form lacks response validation, so Make cannot read customer emails
The scenario schedule is too slow, so it reuses the first response's data
Gmail limits free accounts, so it redirects replies to the sender's address
The owner typed text into To and body instead of mapping the form fields
quiz.x: Typed text is fixed, so every email repeats it; values must be picked from the mapping panel. Validation improves data quality but would not make every email identical.

quiz.q: A yoga instructor in California designs a registration form for an auto-reply. What is the minimum the form must ask for this automation to work as intended?
opts: The person's phone number and the class they want to attend
The person's name, so Gmail can look up the email automatically
The person's name and email address, with the email validated
Just the person's email address, since the name is optional
quiz.x: The email answer tells the automation whom to reply to and the name personalises it; validation helps catch bad emails. Email-only works but loses the personalisation the lab builds.

quiz.q: Before publishing a Zap, Daniel in Lagos clicks Test trigger and gets 'no responses found'. What should he do next?
opts: Submit a test response to the form, then test the trigger again
Switch the trigger to Make, which does not need any test response
Reconnect Gmail, because the action account blocks the trigger test
Publish the Zap anyway, since it will find responses once it is live
quiz.x: Zapier's flow is: choose the form, submit a test response, then Test trigger. Publishing untested risks silent failures, which is the runner-up shortcut.

quiz.q: A Make user has built and tested the scenario with Run once, and the email arrives. A week later no customer has received a reply. What was most likely missed?
opts: Naming the scenario so Make can identify it in the run history
Turning the scenario ON and setting its schedule after testing
Adding response validation so that the form rejects non-emails
Running Run once a second time to confirm the mapping is correct
quiz.x: Run once is a test; the scenario must be switched ON with a schedule to keep watching. Validation is good practice but would not stop every reply.

quiz.q: A Buea training centre expects about 900 form submissions per month, each triggering one email. It is choosing between Zapier and Make free plans. What should it check first?
opts: Each plan's monthly task or operation limits against the expected volume
Whether Gmail allows the centre to send more than one email per hour
Which platform was renamed most recently, since it will be more modern
Which platform has the newest AI features for drafting the reply email
quiz.x: Zapier counts tasks and Make counts operations or credits; free plans have limits that change, so estimate volume first. AI features are secondary to whether the plan can carry the load.

quiz.q: A colleague follows an old blog post that refers to 'Integromat' and is confused because she cannot find it. What should you tell her?
opts: Integromat is the paid tier of Make and needs a separate account
Integromat was renamed Make in 2022, and its concepts carry over
Integromat was discontinued, so the tutorial is no longer useful
Integromat was bought by Zapier, so the tutorial steps now apply there
quiz.x: Integromat became Make in 2022; scenarios, modules and mapping work the same. The Zapier-acquisition story is a plausible but false runner-up.

quiz.q: In the Make scenario, which element is the trigger in the form-to-email automation the module builds?
opts: The mapping panel that supplies the respondent's name and email
The scenario schedule that sets how often Make runs the scenario
Gmail, Send an Email, with the recipient mapped from the form data
Google Forms, Watch Responses, connected to the selected form
quiz.x: Watch Responses detects new submissions and starts the scenario. The schedule controls how often the trigger checks, but the trigger itself is the Forms module.

quiz.q: A US realtor wants one easy auto-reply now; her assistant expects complex chained workflows later on. How does the module compare the two tools?
opts: Make is free with no usage limits, while Zapier has no free plan at all
Both are equivalent, so the choice makes no difference for this business
Zapier is often seen as simplest; Make's visual builder suits multi-step
Zapier is for multi-step flows; Make is limited to one action per flow
quiz.x: The module describes Zapier as often easiest for beginners and Make as a powerful visual builder for multi-step workflows. Saying they are equivalent ignores those real differences.

quiz.q: Esther's form has a free-text email question. Several replies bounce because people typed 'none' or misspelled addresses. What improvement does the module suggest?
opts: Make the name question required so the automation runs more reliably
Send replies from a second Gmail account to reduce the bounce rate
Use response validation on email question to require a valid format
Add a filter in the automation to send replies to Gmail users first
quiz.x: Response validation enforces a valid email format at the source. A filter downstream could skip bad addresses but would not collect the correct ones.

quiz.q: A Zapier user wants to confirm the email action works before publishing. Which step matches the module's Option B sequence?
opts: Click Test action, check inbox, name the Zap, then Publish
Test the trigger alone, since the action is tested when it goes live
Run once, then turn the Zap ON and set how often it checks
Publish first, then submit the form and check the Zap history
quiz.x: Zapier's flow is Test action, check the inbox, name, Publish. 'Run once' and the ON switch are Make's terms, so that option mixes up the platforms.

facts.t: Typing a name or address instead of mapping the form field.
facts.more: Typed text is fixed: every email goes to the same address with the same name. Always pick the value from the mapping panel.

facts.t: Zapier counts tasks; Make counts operations or credits.
facts.more: Free plans have usage limits, and plans change. Estimate monthly volume before building many automations.

facts.t: Minimum form questions for an auto-reply: name and email.
facts.more: The email answer is how the automation knows whom to reply to. Response validation can require a valid email format.

facts.t: Year Integromat was renamed Make.
facts.more: Older tutorials may still say Integromat. The concepts — scenarios, modules, mapping — remain the same.

modules.d: Multi-step workflows, filters, logging, error handling — and your capstone project.
modules.body:
From one automation to a system

Your first automation proved the trigger–action–mapping pattern. Real businesses chain several steps: record every submission, notify the team, route requests to the right person, and follow up automatically. Good design keeps these workflows reliable, understandable and safe.

Common building blocks

  • Logging to Google Sheets: add each submission as a row — a simple database for tracking leads, registrations or orders.
  • Notifications: send yourself or your team a message (email, Slack, Telegram, or SMS via a provider) when something important arrives.
  • Filters: continue only when conditions are met — e.g., only send the VIP email if the budget answer is above a threshold.
  • Routers / paths: send different responses depending on answers — e.g., French speakers receive the French email.
  • Calendar events: create appointments automatically from booking forms.
  • Delays and follow-ups: send a reminder two days later or a follow-up after a week.
  • AI steps: both platforms can call AI models to summarise, classify or draft text inside an automation — powerful, but outputs should be reviewed when they reach customers.

Designing before building

Sketch the workflow on paper or a whiteboard: trigger, each step, conditions, and what happens if something fails. Name each step clearly. Ask: What data does each step need? Where does it come from? Who receives what, in which language? This five-minute sketch prevents hours of rebuilding.

Plan for failure. Automations fail silently if no one is watching: a disconnected account, a changed form question, a full mailbox. Turn on error notifications, check the run history weekly, and test after changing any connected form or sheet. Both Make and Zapier provide execution histories and error alerts — use them.

Data, privacy and trust

Automations move personal data between services. Collect only what you need, tell people how it will be used, restrict access to sheets containing personal data, and remove data you no longer need. Do not send marketing to people who have not agreed. When AI steps process customer messages, check the platform's data terms.

Cost and maintenance

Each step consumes usage units on most plans, and frequently-checking triggers increase usage. Estimate monthly volume before scaling, combine steps where sensible, and document what each automation does and who owns it — so it can be maintained when you are busy or when a team member takes over.

Your capstone project

Complete both builder credentials:

  1. App: your project built through GitHub Actions, installed on a phone, published as a public Release (v1.0.0), with one improvement shipped as v1.0.1 after testing with at least three people, and a README describing the app.
  2. Automation: a working multi-step workflow for a real or realistic business — at minimum a form trigger, a Google Sheets log, a personalised email reply and one filter or route — with a sketch of the design, a test record, error notifications enabled and a short description of how personal data is protected.

Submit links, screenshots and a one-page reflection on what you learned and what you would build next. Your mentor reviews it for functionality, reliability and responsible data use.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my automation architect. I will describe a real business process (e.g., registrations, orders, appointment bookings). Design a multi-step automation: trigger, Google Sheets logging, routing by language or category, personalised emails, follow-up reminders and team notifications. Present it as a step-by-step diagram in text, list the data each step needs, the failure points and how to monitor them, and the privacy safeguards. Then tell me how to build it in [Make or Zapier].

📚 Glossary

  • Filter: condition that must be met for an automation to continue
  • Router / path: branching that sends data down different routes
  • Execution history: log of automation runs and their results
  • Error notification: alert sent when an automation fails
  • Workflow sketch: diagram planning steps before building

📖 References

  • Team21 Academy, No-Code Automation Guide — Next Steps and Advanced Ideas.
  • Make Academy — scenario design, routers and error handling.
  • Zapier Help Center — Filters, Paths and Zap history.
  • Forteh, I. MaDSkillz Training Manual — What to do when you finish.

quiz.q: A Douala event company wants VIP emails sent only when the budget answer exceeds 500,000 FCFA. Which building block handles this?
opts: A delay that waits two days before sending the VIP email to clients
A router that sends every response down both VIP and standard paths
A Sheets log that stores the budget so staff can decide manually
A filter that lets flow continue only when the budget is above it
quiz.x: Filters continue only when conditions are met. A router is the runner-up but is for sending different responses down different paths, not for stopping a flow.

quiz.q: A bilingual Cameroon NGO wants French speakers to get the French email and English speakers the English one, from the same form. What should it use?
opts: An AI step that translates every email after it has been sent out
A router with paths based on the language answer, each with its email
A filter that stops French responses so that staff answer them by hand
Two separate forms, one for each language, each with its own automation
quiz.x: Routers send different responses based on answers, such as language. Two forms work but double maintenance and split the data log.

quiz.q: A Texas clinic's intake automation worked for months, then silently stopped after staff renamed a form question. What practice from the module would have caught this fastest?
opts: Rebuilding the automation every quarter so connections stay fresh
Error notifications plus a weekly check of the run history
Moving to the other platform, which handles renamed questions
Adding an AI step that checks each response before it is processed
quiz.x: Automations fail silently; error alerts and weekly history checks surface problems. Quarterly rebuilds are costly and could still leave months of missed replies.

quiz.q: A Bamenda school's automation uses an AI step to draft replies to parent questions, sent straight to parents. What does the module advise?
opts: Keep it as is, since the platform's AI already filters bad answers
Move the AI step to run after sending so it can log each reply
Remove the AI step, since AI is not allowed in customer automations
Review AI outputs before they reach parents and check data terms
quiz.x: AI steps are powerful but outputs reaching customers should be reviewed, and data terms checked. Banning AI is the over-cautious runner-up the module does not recommend.

quiz.q: An automation runs 3 steps per submission. A business expects 400 submissions per month on a plan with 1,000 operations per month. Assuming each step uses one operation, what is the situation?
opts: About 400 operations, so it fits with room for about 600 more each month
About 800 operations, so it fits as long as the trigger checks less often
About 1,200 operations, so it exceeds the plan and needs redesign or upgrade
About 1,000 operations, so it uses the plan exactly with nothing to spare
quiz.x: 3 steps x 400 = 1,200, above the 1,000 limit. Counting only submissions (400) is the common mistake; most plans count each step.

quiz.q: A Lagos startup collects leads in a Google Sheet via automation. Which practice best reflects the module's data and privacy guidance?
opts: Collect only needed data, restrict sheet access and delete old data
Share the sheet publicly so the team can work faster on new leads
Collect every detail possible now, since data may be useful later
Send marketing to all leads, since they shared their email already
quiz.x: Data minimisation, restricted access and deletion protect people. Marketing without consent is a tempting but wrong runner-up; sharing an email is not agreement to marketing.

quiz.q: Before building a 7-step booking automation, a New York consultant wants to avoid rework. What does the module recommend first?
opts: Build the first two steps and test them before planning the rest
Pick the platform with the most app integrations and start building there
Sketch trigger, steps, conditions and failure paths on paper first
Copy a popular template and adapt it as problems appear in runs
quiz.x: A five-minute sketch of data, recipients, languages and failure paths saves hours. Building incrementally is good testing practice but without a plan it often causes rebuilding.

quiz.q: A capstone learner submits a form trigger, a Sheets log and a personal email. Which minimum component is still missing from the four required?
opts: A calendar event created from each booking submission
A filter or router that changes the flow based on answers
A delay that sends a follow-up reminder one week later
An AI step that summarises each new submission for staff
quiz.x: The capstone minimum is form trigger, Sheets log, personal email and a filter or route. Delays and AI are valid blocks but not among the four required.

quiz.q: After testing her capstone automation with three people, Zainab fixes the confusing parts. How should she release the improvement?
opts: Wait until ten people test it before releasing any change
Ship it as v2.0.0, since user testing changed the design
Keep it at v1.0.0, since just the wording was improved
Ship it as v1.0.1, completing one build, measure, learn loop
quiz.x: The capstone requires one improvement shipped after testing, as a patch v1.0.1. v2.0.0 signals breaking change, which overstates a fix.

quiz.q: A US nonprofit's automation is owned by a volunteer who is leaving next month. What does the module suggest to keep it maintainable?
opts: Document what it does and who owns it, then hand over ownership
Turn it off until a new volunteer can rebuild it from the start
Move it to a personal account so the volunteer can keep it running
Combine every step into one so there is less for others to learn
quiz.x: Documentation of purpose and ownership keeps automations maintainable when people change. Combining steps can save usage but does not transfer knowledge.

facts.t: A paper sketch before building saves hours of rework.
facts.more: Draw trigger, steps, conditions and failure paths. Ask what data each step needs and who receives what, in which language.

facts.t: Automations break without telling anyone unless you set alerts.
facts.more: Disconnected accounts, renamed form questions and full mailboxes stop runs. Turn on error notifications and check run history weekly.

facts.t: The capstone requires one improvement shipped after testing.
facts.more: Test with at least three people, fix what confused them, release a patch — the build–measure–learn loop.

facts.t: Capstone automation: form trigger, Sheets log, personal email, filter/route.
facts.more: Plus a design sketch, a test record, error notifications and a short description of how personal data is protected.
